title: Election Security—or the Engineering of Distrust?
author: Ervin Hoskins
content:
By turning voting machines, classified intelligence, and alleged foreign
interference into [political](https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/policy-
solutions/securing-2024-election) theater, the Trump administration is
preparing voters to distrust an election that has not yet taken place.

Donald Trump has never treated elections simply as contests to be won or lost.
He treats them as tests of
[legitimacy](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/how-do-we-build-trust-in-
elections) whose results are valid only when they confirm his political
authority. His planned national address on the “integrity” of voting machines
therefore should not be dismissed as another attempt to relitigate the 2020
election. It may represent something more consequential: an effort to
establish, before the 2026 midterms, a rationale for challenging any result
unfavorable to Republicans.

The issue is not whether election systems should be protected. They should.
Foreign governments have sought to influence American voters, spread
disinformation, and deepen existing political divisions. Voting equipment,
like every form of [critical](https://www.cisa.gov/topics/election-security)
infrastructure, also requires testing, oversight, and investment.

But election security becomes election sabotage when the government uses the
language and institutions of national security to manufacture
[suspicion](https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/what-does-it-mean-to-ensure-
election-integrity-in-2024) without presenting credible evidence.

The Trump administration’s emerging campaign reportedly goes beyond a
presidential speech. A White House task force has been reviewing classified
intelligence and law-enforcement material concerning alleged election
irregularities. Officials have considered releasing selected intelligence
about foreign efforts to influence the 2020 election. At the same time, the
federal government has increased pressure on state and local election
authorities and expanded its
[scrutiny](https://www.eac.gov/sites/default/files/electionofficials/security/Best_Practices_for_Election_Technology_508.pdf)
of election administration.

Each step can be defended separately as a security measure. Taken together—and
placed in the context of Trump’s continued refusal to acknowledge the
legitimacy of his 2020 defeat—they suggest a political
[strategy](https://www.cisa.gov/topics/election-security): create an
atmosphere in which a future Republican loss appears suspicious before a
single ballot is counted.

That strategy depends on blurring a crucial distinction between foreign
influence and the technical manipulation of votes.

The [National ](https://www.dni.gov/files/ODNI/documents/assessments/ICA-
declass-16MAR21.pdf)Intelligence Council’s 2021 assessment found no indication
that a foreign actor attempted to alter “any technical aspect” of the voting
process, including voter registration, ballot casting, vote tabulation, or the
reporting of results. Reviews by the Justice Department and Department of
Homeland Security reached similar conclusions. Most votes are also
[backed](https://verifiedvoting.org/verifier/) by paper records that allow
officials to audit electronic totals.

Technical vulnerabilities can exist without proving a stolen election. A
responsible administration would explain that difference carefully. It would
identify specific risks, provide evidence, work with state officials, and
propose practical remedies. It would not use a prime-time presidential address
to place an entire electoral system under a cloud of generalized
vulnerability.

This is not transparency. It is political curation backed by the authority of
the intelligence community.

Applying that model to domestic elections would cross a dangerous line.
Intelligence agencies possess extraordinary powers because they are supposed
to defend the country from genuine threats—not determine which election
outcomes citizens should trust. When intelligence becomes ammunition in a
president’s campaign against an anticipated defeat, national security
institutions cease to act as neutral guardians and become participants in a
struggle over political legitimacy.

The objective would not need to be proving fraud. It might be enough to keep
allegations alive.

That is the central political utility of election conspiracy theories. They do
not require most Americans to accept one detailed account of how an election
was stolen. They require only enough uncertainty to persuade millions that no
adverse result can be considered final. Suspicion becomes the product, not an
unfortunate side effect.

This approach also hands foreign adversaries an extraordinary victory. The
most effective attack on an election is not necessarily changing votes. It is
persuading citizens that their votes no longer matter. If the White House
amplifies unproven claims, exaggerates ambiguous intelligence, and portrays
election officials as possible conspirators, it completes the work that
foreign disinformation campaigns seek to
[accomplish](https://www.poynter.org/fact-checking/media-
literacy/2024/election-misinformation-is-rampant-heres-how-to-avoid-it).

Protecting elections requires vigilance against foreign interference. It also
requires vigilance against a government willing to turn that threat into a
weapon against democracy at home.

The post [Election Security—or the Engineering of
Distrust?](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/04/election-security-or-the-
engineering-of-distrust/) appeared first on
[CounterPunch.org](https://www.counterpunch.org).
